claim: TA-G is rapidly deglucosylated in the insect gut of Melolontha melolontha.
source: We have demonstrated that TA-G is rapidly deglucosylated and conjugated to glutathione in the insect gut.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and Figure 1A shows TA-G disappearing and TA appearing in larval gut samples.

claim: TA-G is conjugated to glutathione in the insect gut of Melolontha melolontha.
source: We have demonstrated that TA-G is rapidly deglucosylated and conjugated to glutathione in the insect gut.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, and Figure 1B-C shows TA-GSH and TA-Cys conjugates identified in larvae.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 is a broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase.
source: A broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase, Mm_bGlc17, is sufficient and necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 3C shows Mm_bGlc17 hydrolyzes multiple substrates including TA-G, benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 is sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation.
source: A broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase, Mm_bGlc17, is sufficient and necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 3C shows heterologously expressed Mm_bGlc17 hydrolyzes TA-G in vitro.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 is necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
source: A broad-spectrum M. melolontha β-glucosidase, Mm_bGlc17, is sufficient and necessary for TA-G deglucosylation.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4A shows that silencing Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G deglucosylation by 75% in gut extracts.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G toxicity.
source: Using cross-species RNA interference, we have shown that Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G toxicity.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4B shows that Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae have reduced growth on TA-G-containing plants compared to controls.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 is required for the preference of M. melolontha larvae for TA-G-deficient plants.
source: Furthermore, Mm_bGlc17 is required for the preference of M. melolontha larvae for TA-G-deficient plants.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 4D shows that GFP-control larvae prefer TA-G-deficient plants while Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae show no preference.

claim: Herbivore metabolism modulates both the toxicity and deterrence of a plant defense compound.
source: Thus, herbivore metabolism modulates both the toxicity and deterrence of a plant defense compound.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the combined findings that Mm_bGlc17 affects both larval growth (toxicity) and feeding preference (deterrence).

claim: TA-G deters M. melolontha feeding.
source: The most abundant latex compound, the sesquiterpene lactone glucoside taraxinic acid (TA) β-D-glucopyranosyl ester (TA-G), deters M. melolontha feeding and thereby benefits plant fitness (Huber et al., 2016a; Huber et al., 2016b; Huber et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies showing TA-G deters feeding, and Figure 4D shows control larvae avoid TA-G-containing plants.

claim: TA-G benefits plant fitness.
source: The most abundant latex compound, the sesquiterpene lactone glucoside taraxinic acid (TA) β-D-glucopyranosyl ester (TA-G), deters M. melolontha feeding and thereby benefits plant fitness (Huber et al., 2016a; Huber et al., 2016b; Huber et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies demonstrating this relationship.

claim: The aglycone TA was not detected in T. officinale latex.
source: The aglycone TA was not detected in the latex itself but was present in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed larvae.
evidence: Figure 1A shows TA is absent in latex but present in larval samples.

claim: TA was present in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
source: The aglycone TA was not detected in the latex itself but was present in substantial amounts in the regurgitant and gut of latex-fed larvae.
evidence: Figure 1A shows high levels of TA in regurgitant and gut samples from latex-fed larvae.

claim: TA-G disappeared as soon as the latex was ingested by M. melolontha larvae.
source: TA-G on the other hand disappeared as soon as the latex was ingested by the larvae (Figure 1A).
evidence: Figure 1A shows TA-G is present in latex but absent in larval samples.

claim: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) was identified in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
source: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) and TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) were also identified in latex-fed larvae based on mass spectral and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, with the Cys sulfhydryl moiety being conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: Figure 1B shows TA-GSH peaks in HPLC-MS analysis, and NMR data in supplementary figures confirm structure.

claim: TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) was identified in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
source: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) and TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) were also identified in latex-fed larvae based on mass spectral and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, with the Cys sulfhydryl moiety being conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: Figure 1B shows TA-Cys peaks in HPLC-MS analysis, and NMR data in supplementary figures confirm structure.

claim: The Cys sulfhydryl moiety is conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety.
source: TA-glutathione (TA-GSH) and TA-cysteine (TA-Cys) were also identified in latex-fed larvae based on mass spectral and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, with the Cys sulfhydryl moiety being conjugated to TA at the exocyclic methylene group of the α-methylene-γ-lactone moiety (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: NMR data in Figure 1—figure supplements 2-6 show the chemical structure and conjugation site.

claim: Lower amounts of TA-Cys-Glu and TA-Cys-Gly were present in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
source: Lower amounts of TA-Cys-Glu and TA-Cys-Gly were also present (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows these metabolites detected in larval samples.

claim: No TA-G-GSH or TA-G-Cys conjugates were detected in latex-fed M. melolontha larvae.
source: No TA-G-GSH or TA-G-Cys conjugates were detected in this experiment.
evidence: The text explicitly states these conjugates were not detected in the experiment.

claim: TA is likely first conjugated to GSH and then cleaved sequentially to form other metabolites in M. melolontha.
source: Based on current knowledge of the GSH pathway in insects (Schramm et al., 2012), it is likely that TA is first conjugated to GSH and then cleaved sequentially to form the other metabolites, although some conjugation to GSH prior to deglucosylation may also occur (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from known GSH pathways in insects and the metabolites detected.

claim: Approximately 25% of the ingested TA-G was converted to GSH conjugates and derivatives in M. melolontha.
source: Quantitative measurements showed that approximately 25% of the ingested TA-G was converted to GSH conjugates and derivatives (Figure 1D), with TA-Cys accounting for 95% of all identified compounds (Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1D shows quantitative distribution of metabolites in different body parts.

claim: TA-Cys accounts for 95% of all identified TA-G metabolite compounds in M. melolontha.
source: Quantitative measurements showed that approximately 25% of the ingested TA-G was converted to GSH conjugates and derivatives (Figure 1D), with TA-Cys accounting for 95% of all identified compounds (Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1E shows the relative proportions of different metabolites.

claim: TA-Cys mainly accumulated in the anterior midgut of M. melolontha.
source: TA-Cys mainly accumulated in the anterior midgut (Figure 1D), and this pattern was stable over prolonged exposure of M. melolontha to TA-G (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the highest concentration of metabolites in the anterior midgut.

claim: The pattern of TA-Cys accumulation in the anterior midgut was stable over prolonged exposure of M. melolontha to TA-G.
source: TA-Cys mainly accumulated in the anterior midgut (Figure 1D), and this pattern was stable over prolonged exposure of M. melolontha to TA-G (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 7 shows consistent distribution over time.

claim: The frass of M. melolontha only contained a small fraction of TA conjugates.
source: In contrast to the different body parts, the frass only contained a small fraction of TA conjugates and was dominated by trace quantities of intact TA-G (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Figure 1D-E shows very low levels of metabolites in frass.

claim: The frass of M. melolontha was dominated by trace quantities of intact TA-G.
source: In contrast to the different body parts, the frass only contained a small fraction of TA conjugates and was dominated by trace quantities of intact TA-G (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Figure 1D-E shows TA-G is the main compound in frass.

claim: The deglucosylation and GSH conjugation of TA is a major route for metabolism of this sesquiterpene lactone in M. melolontha.
source: Thus, the deglucosylation and GSH conjugation of TA is a major route for metabolism of this sesquiterpene lactone in M. melolontha.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the quantitative data showing 25% conversion to GSH conjugates.

claim: TA-G in T. officinale latex was readily enzymatically deglucosylated to TA at a pH of 4.6 and 5.4.
source: TA-G in T. officinale latex incubated at different pH levels at room temperature was readily enzymatically deglucosylated to TA at a pH of 4.6 and 5.4, but not at lower or higher pH values (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows high deglucosylation activity at pH 4.6 and 5.4.

claim: TA-G in T. officinale latex was not enzymatically deglucosylated at pH values lower than 4.6 or higher than 5.4.
source: TA-G in T. officinale latex incubated at different pH levels at room temperature was readily enzymatically deglucosylated to TA at a pH of 4.6 and 5.4, but not at lower or higher pH values (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows minimal deglucosylation activity outside the pH 4.6-5.4 range.

claim: The midgut pH of M. melolontha is above 8.
source: As the midgut pH of M. melolontha is above 8 (Figure 2B; Egert et al., 2005), the deglucosylation of TA-G by plant-derived enzymes is likely inhibited.
evidence: Figure 2B shows pH data, and Egert et al., 2005 is cited as a reference.

claim: The deglucosylation of TA-G by plant-derived enzymes is likely inhibited in the M. melolontha midgut.
source: As the midgut pH of M. melolontha is above 8 (Figure 2B; Egert et al., 2005), the deglucosylation of TA-G by plant-derived enzymes is likely inhibited.
evidence: This is inferred from the mismatch between plant enzyme pH optimum (4.6-5.4) and gut pH (>8).

claim: Strong deglucosylation activity was detected in the proximal parts of the M. melolontha gut, especially in the anterior midgut.
source: Strong deglucosylation activity was detected in the proximal parts of the gut, especially in the anterior midgut (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows highest deglucosylation activity in anterior midgut extracts.

claim: TA-G hydrolysis occurred when M. melolontha larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex.
source: TA-G hydrolysis also occurred when larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex, which no longer hydrolyzes TA-G itself (Figure 2A and C), and the presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows TA formation in larvae fed heat-deactivated latex.

claim: Heat-deactivated T. officinale latex no longer hydrolyzes TA-G.
source: TA-G hydrolysis also occurred when larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex, which no longer hydrolyzes TA-G itself (Figure 2A and C), and the presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2A shows no deglucosylation in boiled latex samples.

claim: The presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins.
source: TA-G hydrolysis also occurred when larvae were fed with a diet containing heat-deactivated latex, which no longer hydrolyzes TA-G itself (Figure 2A and C), and the presence of TA-G-hydrolyzing latex proteins in TA-G-containing diets did not result in higher amounts of TA or TA conjugates inside M. melolontha compared to diets with heat-deactivated latex proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows no significant difference in TA or conjugate levels between intact and heat-deactivated latex treatments.

claim: Insect-derived enzymes are sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
source: Therefore, insect-derived enzymes are sufficient for TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing TA-G hydrolysis occurs with heat-deactivated plant enzymes.

claim: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner.
source: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner, but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2 show dose-dependent inhibition by castanospermine.

claim: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was not inhibited by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose.
source: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner, but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows no inhibition by acarbose.

claim: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was not inhibited by the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate.
source: TA-G deglucosylation by M. melolontha midgut protein extracts was inhibited by the addition of the α- and β-glucosidase inhibitor castanospermine in a dose-dependent manner, but not by the α-glucosidase inhibitor acarbose or the carboxylesterase inhibitor bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows no inhibition by bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate.

claim: β-glucosidases rather than carboxylesterases catalyze TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
source: This suggests that β-glucosidases rather than carboxylesterases catalyze TA-G deglucosylation in M. melolontha.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the inhibitor studies showing only glucosidase inhibitors are effective.

claim: 19 sequences similar to β-glucosidases had an expression profile matching the observed pattern of high TA-G deglucosylation activity in the anterior midgut of M. melolontha.
source: 19 sequences similar to β-glucosidases had an expression profile matching the observed pattern of high TA-G deglucosylation activity in the anterior midgut.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the transcriptome analysis.

claim: 12 full-length β-glucosidases were amplified from M. melolontha cDNA sharing between 55 and 79% amino acid similarity.
source: Partial sequences were extended using rapid-amplification of complementary DNA (cDNA) ends polymerase chain reaction (RACE PCR), resulting in 12 full-length β-glucosidases sharing between 55 and 79% amino acid similarity (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Figure 3A shows the phylogenetic tree of the 12 β-glucosidases.

claim: All amplified M. melolontha β-glucosidase sequences contained an N-terminal excretion signal.
source: All amplified sequences contained an N-terminal excretion signal and possessed the ITENG and NEP motifs characteristic of glucosidases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Sanz-Aparicio et al., 1998; Davies and Henrissat, 1995; Barrett et al., 1995).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the sequence alignment with signal peptides.

claim: All amplified M. melolontha β-glucosidase sequences possessed the ITENG and NEP motifs characteristic of glucosidases.
source: All amplified sequences contained an N-terminal excretion signal and possessed the ITENG and NEP motifs characteristic of glucosidases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Sanz-Aparicio et al., 1998; Davies and Henrissat, 1995; Barrett et al., 1995).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows these conserved motifs in the alignment.

claim: Expression levels of the candidate M. melolontha β-glucosidase genes were 37- to 308-fold higher in the anterior than posterior midgut samples.
source: Expression levels of the candidate genes were 37- to 308-fold higher in the anterior than posterior midgut samples (padj <10–5, exact tests, n = 3), thus matching the differences in TA-G deglucosylation rate between these gut compartments (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows the heat map of expression levels in different gut sections.

claim: Average expression of the M. melolontha β-glucosidase transcripts did not differ among larvae fed water, TA-G, or latex.
source: Average expression of the transcripts did not differ among M. melolontha larvae fed water, TA-G, or latex (Figure 3B; padj >0.50, exact tests, n = 3).
evidence: Figure 3B shows similar expression levels across different diet treatments.

claim: 9 of the 12 heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases were active with the standard fluorogenic substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-D-glucopyranoside.
source: 9 of the 12 β-glucosidases were active with the standard fluorogenic substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-D-glucopyranoside, and hydrolyzed at least one of the plant metabolites (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 3C shows activity with Glc-MU for 9 enzymes.

claim: 9 of the 12 heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases hydrolyzed at least one of the plant metabolites tested.
source: 9 of the 12 β-glucosidases were active with the standard fluorogenic substrate, 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-D-glucopyranoside, and hydrolyzed at least one of the plant metabolites (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 3C shows substrate specificity for different plant glycosides.

claim: All tested plant glycoside substrates were deglucosylated by at least one M. melolontha glucosidase.
source: All tested substrates were deglucosylated by at least one M. melolontha glucosidase (Figure 3C) in agreement with the hydrolysis activity of crude midgut extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 3C shows that each substrate column has at least one positive result.

claim: Five heterologously expressed M. melolontha proteins deglucosylated TA-G.
source: Five heterologously expressed proteins deglucosylated TA-G (Figure 3C), with the highest TA aglycone formation found for Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 3C shows five enzymes with TA-G activity.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 showed the highest TA aglycone formation among heterologously expressed M. melolontha β-glucosidases.
source: Five heterologously expressed proteins deglucosylated TA-G (Figure 3C), with the highest TA aglycone formation found for Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 4 shows Mm_bGlc17 produces the most TA.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 deglyosylated benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose in addition to TA-G.
source: Apart from TA-G, Mm_bGlc17 also deglyosylated benzoxazinoids, salicin, and cellobiose.
evidence: Figure 3C shows Mm_bGlc17 activity with multiple substrates.

claim: Silencing of Mm_bGlc17 resulted in a stable and specific reduction of the target mRNA after 5 days.
source: After 5 days, a stable and specific reduction of the target mRNAs had occurred (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3 show reduced Mm_bGlc17 expression in silenced larvae.

claim: TA-G deglucosylation was reduced by 75% in gut extracts of M. melolontha larvae that were silenced in Mm_bGlc17.
source: TA-G deglucosylation was reduced by 75% in gut extracts of larvae that were silenced in Mm_bGlc17 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows significantly reduced deglucosylation activity in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae.

claim: Silencing of Mm_bGlc16 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to GFP controls.
source: Silencing of Mm_bGlc16 and Mm_bGlu18 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to green fluorescent protein (GFP) controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows no significant difference between Mm_bGlc16-silenced and GFP control larvae.

claim: Silencing of Mm_bGlc18 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to GFP controls.
source: Silencing of Mm_bGlc16 and Mm_bGlu18 did not significantly reduce TA-G deglucosylation activity compared to green fluorescent protein (GFP) controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows no significant difference between Mm_bGlc18-silenced and GFP control larvae.

claim: Mm_Glc17 accounts for most of the TA-G deglucosylation in vivo in M. melolontha.
source: These results confirm that M. melolontha-derived β-glucosidases hydrolyze TA-G and demonstrate that Mm_Glc17 accounts for most of the TA-G deglucosylation in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the 75% reduction in activity when Mm_bGlc17 is silenced.

claim: The interaction of Mm_bGlc17 silencing and plant genotype significantly affected M. melolontha larval growth.
source: The interaction of Mm_bGlc17 silencing and plant genotype significantly affected larval growth (Figure 4B; p(Mm_bGlc17 x TA-G) = 0.009, two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)).
evidence: Figure 4B shows the statistical interaction between enzyme silencing and plant genotype on growth.

claim: On TA-G-containing plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing reduced M. melolontha larval growth.
source: On TA-G-containing plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing reduced larval growth, with GFP-control larvae gaining 4.5% body weight and Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae losing 1.4% body weight (Figure 4B; p = 0.009, Student's t-test).
evidence: Figure 4B shows reduced weight gain in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae on wild-type plants.

claim: On TA-G-deficient plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not affect M. melolontha larval weight gain.
source: By contrast, on TA-G-deficient plants, Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not affect larval weight gain (p = 0.19, Student's t-test).
evidence: Figure 4B shows no significant difference in growth on TA-G-deficient plants.

claim: GFP-control M. melolontha larvae had higher growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants.
source: GFP-control M. melolontha larvae had higher growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants (p = 0.035, Student's t-test; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), while the reversed pattern was found in tendency for Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae (p = 0.099, Student's t-test; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4 show this growth pattern.

claim: Mm_bGlc17-silenced M. melolontha larvae showed a tendency for lower growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants.
source: GFP-control M. melolontha larvae had higher growth on TA-G-containing than TA-G-lacking plants (p = 0.035, Student's t-test; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), while the reversed pattern was found in tendency for Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae (p = 0.099, Student's t-test; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 4 shows this trend.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 gene expression increased by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants.
source: Mm_bGlc17 gene expression increased by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants (Figure 4C; p = 0.04, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Figure 4C shows higher Mm_bGlc17 expression on wild-type plants.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 expression is induced by TA-G.
source: As Mm_bGlc17 benefited larval growth in the presence of TA-G, we investigated whether the expression of this gene is induced by TA-G. Mm_bGlc17 gene expression increased by 95% on TA-G-containing compared to TA-G-lacking plants (Figure 4C; p = 0.04, Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Figure 4C shows increased expression in the presence of TA-G.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 increases M. melolontha larval performance in the presence of TA-G.
source: Taken together, these data show that Mm_bGlc17 expression is induced by TA-G and increases larval performance in the presence of TA-G.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the growth data showing Mm_bGlc17 benefits larvae on TA-G-containing plants.

claim: GFP-silenced control M. melolontha larvae were deterred by TA-G.
source: GFP-silenced control larvae were deterred by TA-G, with over 60% of the larvae feeding on TA-G-deficient plants and 30-% on the wild-type (Figure 4D; p(3h) = 0.006, binomial test).
evidence: Figure 4D shows GFP-control larvae preferentially chose TA-G-deficient plants.

claim: Mm_bGlc17-silenced M. melolontha larvae did not show any preference for TA-G-deficient over TA-G-producing wild-type plants.
source: By contrast, Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae did not show any preference for TA-G-deficient over TA-G-producing wild-type plants: 44% of the larvae fed on wild-type plants, while 42% fed on TA-G-deficient plants (Figure 4D; p(3h) = 0.86, binomial test).
evidence: Figure 4D shows no significant preference in Mm_bGlc17-silenced larvae.

claim: The choice patterns of M. melolontha larvae between TA-G-deficient and wild-type plants were constant over time.
source: Both patterns were constant over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 6 shows stable choice patterns over 4 hours.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not significantly affect the total percentage of M. melolontha larvae that made a choice.
source: Mm_bGlc17 silencing did not significantly affect the total percentage of larvae that made a choice (86% Mm_bGlc17 vs 91% GFP).
evidence: The text provides the percentages showing similar choice rates.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 expression is required for the deterrent effect of TA-G toward M. melolontha.
source: These results demonstrate that Mm_bGlc17 expression is required for the deterrent effect of TA-G toward M. melolontha.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the choice experiment showing loss of deterrence when Mm_bGlc17 is silenced.

claim: A major metabolization product of TA-G is TA-Cys, with about 25% of the ingested TA-G accumulating in this form.
source: A major metabolization product of TA-G is TA-Cys, with about 25% of the ingested TA-G accumulating in this form.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the quantitative data in Figure 1.

claim: It is likely that TA-G is deglucosylated prior conjugation to GSH and subsequently sequentially cleaved to TA-Cys by peptidases.
source: Based on our current knowledge of the GSH pathway in insects (Schramm et al., 2012), it is likely that TA-G is deglucosylated prior conjugation to GSH and subsequently sequentially cleaved to TA-Cys by peptidases.
evidence: This is inferred from known GSH pathways and the metabolites detected.

claim: The first step of TA-G metabolization, the conjugation of GSH to TA, may occur spontaneously and/or via GSH glucosyl-transferases.
source: The first step of this metabolization pathway, the conjugation of GSH to TA, may occur spontaneously and/or via GSH glucosyl-transferases.
evidence: This is speculated based on the chemistry of the reaction.

claim: When TA and TA-G were incubated with high concentrations of GSH and Cys in vitro, several isomers of the conjugates formed that were not detected inside the M. melolontha gut.
source: When we incubated TA and TA-G with high concentrations of GSH and Cys in vitro, several isomers of the conjugates formed that were not detected inside the M. melolontha gut, suggesting that enzymatic rather than spontaneous conjugation of GSH to TA prevails inside the larva.
evidence: This observation is described in the discussion.

claim: Enzymatic rather than spontaneous conjugation of GSH to TA prevails inside the M. melolontha larva.
source: When we incubated TA and TA-G with high concentrations of GSH and Cys in vitro, several isomers of the conjugates formed that were not detected inside the M. melolontha gut, suggesting that enzymatic rather than spontaneous conjugation of GSH to TA prevails inside the larva.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between in vitro and in vivo conjugate profiles.

claim: M. melolontha larvae must further metabolize TA-Cys to yet unknown products.
source: Interestingly, TA-Cys mostly accumulated in the anterior midgut, and only neglectable amounts of TA-Cys were excreted by the larvae, a pattern that was stable over long-term feeding of M. melolontha on T. officinale. Consequently, larvae must further metabolize TA-Cys to yet unknown products, and either store or excrete these compounds.
evidence: This is inferred from the low excretion of TA-Cys despite its accumulation.

claim: Transformation of defense metabolites by insect enyzmes occurs in the gut.
source: As the transformation of defense metabolites by insect enyzmes occurs in the gut, metabolization products are considered unlikely to be tasted via frontal sensory structures of insect herbivores.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Metabolization products of plant defense compounds are considered unlikely to be tasted via frontal sensory structures of insect herbivores.
source: As the transformation of defense metabolites by insect enyzmes occurs in the gut, metabolization products are considered unlikely to be tasted via frontal sensory structures of insect herbivores. It is thus commonly assumed that there is no direct impact of this process on herbivore behavior (Pentzold et al., 2014; Simon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited as a common assumption in the field.

claim: It is commonly assumed that there is no direct impact of insect-mediated defense metabolite transformation on herbivore behavior.
source: As the transformation of defense metabolites by insect enyzmes occurs in the gut, metabolization products are considered unlikely to be tasted via frontal sensory structures of insect herbivores. It is thus commonly assumed that there is no direct impact of this process on herbivore behavior (Pentzold et al., 2014; Simon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited as a common assumption that the current study challenges.

claim: Transformation of defense metabolites by plant enzymes that are activated by tissue disruption is well accepted to have a strong behavioral impact on insect herbivores.
source: By contrast, transformation of defense metabolites by plant enzymes that are activated by tissue disruption is well accepted to have a strong behavioral impact on insect herbivores, which is in line with the rapid and early formation of plant defense catabolites (Glauser et al., 2011; Krothapalli et al., 2013; de Vos et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2006; Mumm et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The insect β-glucosidase Mm_bGlc17 is required to elicit the deterrent effect of TA-G.
source: Here, we have found that the insect β-glucosidase Mm_bGlc17, which deglucosylates a defensive sesquiterpene lactone (TA-G) in the insect gut, is also required to elicit the deterrent effect of this metabolite.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the choice experiment data.

claim: The capacity of dandelions to produce TA-G reduces M. melolontha attack in a community context.
source: Our early work on TA-G showed that, in a community context, the capacity of dandelions to produce the glucosylated sesquiterpene lactone reduces M. melolontha attack and its negative effect on plant growth and fitness (Huber et al., 2016b), resulting in the selection of high TA-G genotypes under high M. melolontha pressure (Huber et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: The capacity of dandelions to produce TA-G reduces the negative effect of M. melolontha on plant growth and fitness.
source: Our early work on TA-G showed that, in a community context, the capacity of dandelions to produce the glucosylated sesquiterpene lactone reduces M. melolontha attack and its negative effect on plant growth and fitness (Huber et al., 2016b), resulting in the selection of high TA-G genotypes under high M. melolontha pressure (Huber et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: High M. melolontha pressure results in the selection of high TA-G genotypes in dandelions.
source: Our early work on TA-G showed that, in a community context, the capacity of dandelions to produce the glucosylated sesquiterpene lactone reduces M. melolontha attack and its negative effect on plant growth and fitness (Huber et al., 2016b), resulting in the selection of high TA-G genotypes under high M. melolontha pressure (Huber et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: The effects of TA-G on dandelion fitness are likely the result of the deterrent, rather than the toxic properties of TA-G.
source: As these effects are likely the result of the deterrent, rather than the toxic properties of TA-G, they are likely also directly dependent on the presence of Mm_bGlc17.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that Mm_bGlc17 is required for deterrence.

claim: The effects of TA-G on dandelion fitness are likely directly dependent on the presence of Mm_bGlc17.
source: As these effects are likely the result of the deterrent, rather than the toxic properties of TA-G, they are likely also directly dependent on the presence of Mm_bGlc17.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of Mm_bGlc17 in mediating deterrence.

claim: The metabolism of M. melolontha may drive the feeding preferences of the herbivore.
source: Thus, the metabolism of M. melolontha may not only drive the feeding preferences of the herbivore, but also the ecology and evolution of dandelions in their natural habitat.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings on Mm_bGlc17's role in deterrence.

claim: The metabolism of M. melolontha may drive the ecology and evolution of dandelions in their natural habitat.
source: Thus, the metabolism of M. melolontha may not only drive the feeding preferences of the herbivore, but also the ecology and evolution of dandelions in their natural habitat.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects on herbivore behavior and plant fitness.

claim: Insect-detoxifying enzymes may shape plant defense evolution by modulating herbivore host plant choice.
source: Insect-detoxifying enzymes may thus shape plant defense evolution not only by reducing the toxicity of defense compounds but also by modulating herbivore host plant choice.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Many plant defensive metabolites are glycosides, which are typically non-toxic themselves but are deglucosylated upon herbivore damage, forming toxic products.
source: Many plant defensive metabolites are glycosides, which are typically non-toxic themselves but are deglucosylated upon herbivore damage, forming toxic products.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Both plant- and herbivore-derived β-glucosidases can mediate deglycosylation in the insect gut.
source: Both plant- and herbivore-derived β-glucosidases can mediate deglycosylation in the insect gut, but their relative contribution is often unclear (Pentzold et al., 2014; Desroches et al., 1997; Lindroth, 1988; Pankoke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The relative contribution of plant- and herbivore-derived β-glucosidases to deglycosylation in the insect gut is often unclear.
source: Both plant- and herbivore-derived β-glucosidases can mediate deglycosylation in the insect gut, but their relative contribution is often unclear (Pentzold et al., 2014; Desroches et al., 1997; Lindroth, 1988; Pankoke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The deglucosylation of TA-G depends primarily on β-glucosidases from M. melolontha rather than on plant enzymes.
source: Here we provide several parallel lines of evidence to demonstrate that the deglucosylation of TA-G, a glucosylated secondary metabolite in the latex of T. officinale, depends primarily on β-glucosidases from M. melolontha rather than on plant enzymes.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by multiple lines of evidence presented in the results.

claim: T. officinale TA-G hydrolase activity has an acidic pH optimum (4.8–5.4).
source: First, T. officinale TA-G hydrolase activity has an acidic pH optimum (4.8–5.4), and the activity is very low at the alkaline pH (8.0) found in the gut of M. melolontha.
evidence: Figure 2A shows pH-dependent activity of plant enzymes.

claim: T. officinale TA-G hydrolase activity is very low at the alkaline pH (8.0) found in the gut of M. melolontha.
source: First, T. officinale TA-G hydrolase activity has an acidic pH optimum (4.8–5.4), and the activity is very low at the alkaline pH (8.0) found in the gut of M. melolontha.
evidence: Figure 2A shows minimal plant enzyme activity at pH 8.

claim: TA-G is deglucosylated by M. melolontha gut extracts in the absence of plant material.
source: Second, TA-G is deglucosylated by M. melolontha gut extracts in the absence of plant material.
evidence: Figure 2B shows gut extracts hydrolyze TA-G from boiled latex.

claim: M. melolontha expresses several β-glucosidases with TA-G-hydrolyzing activity as demonstrated in in vitro assays.
source: Fourth, M. melolontha expresses several β-glucosidases with TA-G-hydrolyzing activity as demonstrated in in vitro assays.
evidence: Figure 3C shows five β-glucosidases with TA-G activity.

claim: Silencing the M. melolontha TA-G β-glucosidase Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G deglucosylation activity in larval gut extracts.
source: Fifth, silencing the M. melolontha TA-G β-glucosidase Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G deglucosylation activity in larval gut extracts and abolishes the avoidance behavior of M. melolontha toward TA-G-containing plants.
evidence: Figure 4A shows reduced deglucosylation in silenced larvae.

claim: Silencing Mm_bGlc17 abolishes the avoidance behavior of M. melolontha toward TA-G-containing plants.
source: Fifth, silencing the M. melolontha TA-G β-glucosidase Mm_bGlc17 reduces TA-G deglucosylation activity in larval gut extracts and abolishes the avoidance behavior of M. melolontha toward TA-G-containing plants.
evidence: Figure 4D shows loss of preference in silenced larvae.

claim: Insect rather than plant β-glucosidases hydrolyze ingested TA-G in M. melolontha.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that insect rather than plant β-glucosidases hydrolyze ingested TA-G in M. melolontha.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the multiple lines of evidence presented.

claim: Known plant protoxins include glucosinolates, salicinoids, and cyanogenic, iridoid, and benzoxazinoid glycosides.
source: Known plant protoxins include glucosinolates, salicinoids, and cyanogenic, iridoid, and benzoxazinoid glycosides.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Sesquiterpene lactone aglycones are much more potent than their corresponding glycosides in pharmacological studies of cytotoxicity and anti-cancer activity.
source: Sesquiterpene lactone aglycones are much more potent than their corresponding glycosides in pharmacological studies of cytotoxicity and anti-cancer activity (Choi et al., 2002; Seto et al., 1988).
evidence: This is cited from pharmacological studies.

claim: The consequences of sesquiterpene lactone deglycosylation for herbivore behavior and performance have not been previously investigated.
source: However, the consequences of sesquiterpene lactone deglycosylation for herbivore behavior and performance have not been previously investigated (Huber et al., 2015; Sessa et al., 2000; Graziani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Deglucosylation of TA-G is associated with an increase rather than a decrease in larval growth on TA-G-producing plants.
source: Our experiments show that deglucosylation of TA-G is associated with an increase rather than a decrease in larval growth on TA-G-producing plants.
evidence: Figure 4B shows better growth when Mm_bGlc17 is functional.

claim: The cleavage of TA-G to TA reduces rather than enhances the toxicity of this sesquiterpene lactone.
source: This suggests that the cleavage of TA-G to TA reduces rather than enhances the toxicity of this sesquiterpene lactone.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth data showing Mm_bGlc17 benefits larvae.

claim: GSH may be more rapidly conjugated by TA than TA-G.
source: First, GSH may be more rapidly conjugated by TA than TA-G, and thus deglucosylation is a step toward detoxification.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation for the detoxification effect.

claim: If the target site of TA-G lies in a hydrophilic compartment (such as the gut lumen), deglucosylation may block its activity.
source: Second, if the target site of TA-G lies in a hydrophilic compartment (such as the gut lumen), deglucosylation may block its activity.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation for the detoxification effect.

claim: The glucose liberated by TA-G deglucosylation may enhance the nutritional quality of dandelion roots for M. melolontha larvae.
source: Third, the glucose liberated by TA-G deglucosylation may enhance the nutritional quality of dandelion roots for the larvae.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation for better growth on TA-G-containing plants.

claim: Deglycosylation of plant defenses may reduce negative impacts on herbivores.
source: In summary, our results provide evidence that deglycosylation of plant defenses may reduce negative impacts on herbivores.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the growth data from the study.

claim: The recognition of TA-G through deglucosylation may guide the M. melolontha larva to feeding sites that are most suitable for fast larval growth.
source: First, the recognition of TA-G through deglucosylation may guide the M. melolontha larva to feeding sites that are most suitable for fast larval growth, independently of the toxicity of TA-G.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism for the observed behavior.

claim: Exploitation of plant secondary metabolites and sugars to locate nutritious tissue has been reported for Diabrotica virgifera virgifera feeding on maize roots.
source: Exploitation of plant secondary metabolites and sugars to locate nutritious tissue has been reported, for instance, for the specialist root herbivore Diabrotica virgifera virgifera feeding on maize roots (Robert et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2018; Machado et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited as a parallel example from other systems.

claim: M. melolontha larvae preferentially feed on side roots of dandelions.
source: Melolontha melolontha larvae preferentially feed on side roots of dandelions, which contain lower TA-G and higher soluble protein levels than main roots and also may be more nutritious as they are actively growing (Huber et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Side roots of dandelions contain lower TA-G and higher soluble protein levels than main roots.
source: Melolontha melolontha larvae preferentially feed on side roots of dandelions, which contain lower TA-G and higher soluble protein levels than main roots and also may be more nutritious as they are actively growing (Huber et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The larvae may not be avoiding TA-G because of its toxicity, but because avoiding high TA-G levels guides them to nutritious roots.
source: Thus, the larvae may not be avoiding TA-G because of its toxicity, but because avoiding high TA-G levels guides them to nutritious roots, with the avoidance behavior being facilitated by Mm_bGlc17.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative explanation for the observed behavior.

claim: Herbivore growth by itself gives an incomplete picture regarding the costs of TA-G consumption and metabolism.
source: A second explanation for the observed patterns may be that herbivore growth by itself gives an incomplete picture regarding the costs of TA-G consumption and metabolism.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative explanation for the counterintuitive results.

claim: Plant secondary metabolites can enhance larval weight gain, but at the same time increase larval mortality.
source: It has been shown, for instance, that plant secondary metabolites can enhance larval weight gain, but at the same time increase larval mortality, suggesting that growth is not always beneficial (Veyrat et al., 2016; Erb, 2018).
evidence: This is cited as evidence that growth alone doesn't capture all fitness effects.

claim: The hydrolysis of TA-G may deplete the level of cysteine inside the M. melolontha larva through conjugation of TA to glutathione.
source: In addition, the hydrolysis of TA-G may deplete the level of cysteine inside the larva through conjugation of TA to glutathione, as has been observed in lepidopteran larvae that conjugate food-derived isothiocyanates to GSH (Jeschke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is proposed as a possible cost of TA-G metabolism, citing a parallel example.

claim: Under natural conditions, Mm_bGlc17-dependent cleavage of TA-G may reduce rather than enhance M. melolontha fitness.
source: Thus, it is possible that under natural conditions, Mm_bGlc17-dependent cleavage of TA-G reduces rather than enhances M. melolontha fitness, which may explain Mm_bGlc17-mediated TA-G avoidance.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation for the observed avoidance behavior.

claim: Mm_bGlc17 may be maintained in the insect genome if it is important for the larva to acquire nutrients.
source: The gene may, nevertheless, be maintained in the insect genome if Mm_bGlc17 is important for the larva to acquire nutrients.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation for the maintenance of the gene.

claim: Dandelions would exploit a promiscuous β-glucosidase (Mm_bGlc17) whose evolution is constrained by its primary functions in nutrient acquisition.
source: In such a scenario, dandelions would exploit a promiscuous β-glucosidase (Mm_bGlc17) whose evolution is constrained by its primary functions in nutrient acquisition.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible evolutionary scenario.

claim: The ability of Mm_bGlc17 to mediate hydrolysis of a range of glucosides plus the glucose ester TA-G is unusual.
source: The fact that Mm_bGlc17 catalyzes the hydrolysis of a range of glucosides plus the glucose ester TA-G is also unusual. There are only a few previous reports of enzymes with this versatility (Nakano et al., 1998; Okamoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as an unusual feature, citing limited previous examples.

claim: The ability of Mm_bGlc17 to mediate hydrolysis of cellobiose suggests its evolutionary origin as a digestive enzyme that was later recruited for processing plant defenses.
source: The ability of Mm_bGlc17 to mediate hydrolysis of cellobiose, a disaccharide derived from cellulose, suggests its evolutionary origin as a digestive enzyme that was later recruited for processing plant defenses.
evidence: This is inferred from the enzyme's substrate specificity.

claim: The relatively large number of β-glucosidases in many insect herbivores indicates that many β-glucosidases act on a variety of specialized metabolites, such as plant defense compounds.
source: The relatively large number of β-glucosidases in many insect herbivores (Pentzold et al., 2014; Poreddy et al., 2015; Beran et al., 2014) and their species-specific phylogenetic clustering (Beran et al., 2014) indicate that in addition to contributing to the digestion of cell wall carbohydrates—which are mostly shared among plant species—many β-glucosidases also act on a variety of specialized metabolites, such as plant defense compounds.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity and phylogenetic patterns of β-glucosidases.

claim: Plant defenses may play an underestimated role in the evolution of β-glucosidases in insect herbivores.
source: Thus, plant defenses may play an underestimated role in the evolution of β-glucosidases in insect herbivores.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of the study and cited literature.

claim: Other herbivore digestive enzymes may also interact with plant defenses, leading to changes in herbivore performance and behavior.
source: Other herbivore digestive enzymes may also interact with plant defenses, leading to changes in herbivore performance and behavior, which likely modulate the ecology and evolution of plants and their consumers.
evidence: This is a general conclusion extrapolated from the study's findings.

claim: Interactions between herbivore digestive enzymes and plant defenses likely modulate the ecology and evolution of plants and their consumers.
source: Other herbivore digestive enzymes may also interact with plant defenses, leading to changes in herbivore performance and behavior, which likely modulate the ecology and evolution of plants and their consumers.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings.
